title: I used AI to help build a tactical roguelite, and learned why “just prompt the game” does not work
author: Right_Building_8032
selftext:
Hi everyone! I would mainly like to discuss what developing a complete game with AI assistance actually looked like for me.

I have just released **Slime - Gotta Eat'Em All!**, a free-to-play tactical roguelite for Android. Every enemy can be killed, swallowed alive or soothed, and its faction adapts to the way the player wins.

AI was involved throughout development, but this was not a case of entering one large prompt and receiving a finished game.

I used Codex directly inside the Godot project as an engineering and design partner. It helped inspect the repository, implement systems, create automated tests, diagnose regressions, manage data-driven content and iterate on the UI. Generative tools were also used during visual production, while some sound effects were prototyped with an AI audio model before being selected and reworked.

The greatest advantage was iteration speed. I could describe a gameplay problem, such as Swallow being stronger than the other victory paths, and rapidly test several connected changes across rewards, faction adaptation, interface text and tutorials.

The greatest weakness was consistency.

AI could produce something that looked convincing in isolation while completely missing the larger context. Character sprites faced the wrong direction. Accessories looked correct on one body but detached during animations. A metallic effect replaced the original design instead of preserving it. Interface terminology multiplied until the game became difficult to understand. Some “fixes” technically worked but felt wrong when played.

A large part of development therefore became review, rejection and correction. I had to keep asking: does this mechanic create an interesting decision? Does the animation communicate the actual effect? Does the same feature still work with multiple enemies, every faction, mobile input and saved games?

Automated tests were extremely useful, but they were not enough. A test could confirm that a card removed seven Integrity while the player still had no idea why only five points appeared on screen. Visual inspection and real playtesting remained essential.

My main lesson is that AI is very good at expanding the number of possible solutions, but it does not remove the need for direction. In some ways, it increases the need for it. Without a clear visual language, design rules and aggressive testing, the project can become a collection of individually plausible features that do not form a coherent game.

The game is now available here:

**Google Play:** [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.maxde.rogueliteslime](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.maxde.rogueliteslime)

PS : I made updates since the video, so the gameplay is a bit better now, but still improving.

I would be very interested in hearing from other developers using AI:

How do you prevent AI-assisted projects from losing visual or mechanical consistency as they grow? Do you rely mainly on documentation, automated tests, strict asset pipelines, or something else?

I am also happy to answer questions about the development process, including what had to be rebuilt manually after an AI-generated solution failed.

comments.author: scratchieee
comments.body: Man it is like groundhog day, is there anyone not working on an AI tactical roguelike? I see these cookie cutter posts every day and they are always screaming AI. Backgrounds don't match, broken animations/limited animations and generic UI.

replies.author: Right_Building_8032
replies.body: That's the kind of game I like (played "Slay the Spire" again this week), and that it's easier with AI since it doesn't require this much design to work.
